newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage takers agree to join peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage takers agree to join peace talks.

text.p: Talks to end Peru's month-long hostage crisis crept forward on Wednesday as Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home agreed to join a "guarantor" committee to oversee a peaceful solution.

"The proposal to set up a committee is acceptable," Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini said in a radio conversation from within the residence monitored by Reuters.

Education Minister Domingo Palermo, the government negotiator who proposed the committee on Sunday, acknowledged receipt of Cerpa's reply in a brief statement. Further talks between the two sides would remain secret, he added.
Cerpa pledged that the rebels would not "execute" any of their hostages. "It is not in our minds to carry out executions, nor to give any ultimatums," he said. "We have never spoken of executions."

He said the MRTA would accept Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani and a Red Cross representative on the committee as suggested by the government. But the rebels also asked for representation from Guatemala and a European country.
"The place of the meeting is a matter that can be discussed and decided by mutual accord," he added.
Guatemala's Foreign Minister Eduardo Stein said his government would be prepared to help find a solution to the crisis if asked by Peru.

Stein told reporters in Guatemala City that Guatemala's ambassador in Lima Jose Maria Argueta -- himself held hostage at the residence until Dec. 26 -- had been designated to join the talks if called upon.

Despite the apparent step forward in the 29-day crisis, the MRTA claimed real progress was impossible while the government stood fast in its refusal to discuss their chief demand: the release of all their imprisoned comrades.
"The government proposes a peaceful solution but at the same time says it does not have anything to negotiate with us," Cerpa said. Officials have flatly refused any releases.

Cerpa warned that without tangible progress in negotiations the crisis was "being pushed towards a military end" and said the government would be to blame for any injury to hostages in a possible storming of the residence.

The rebel leader also told the government his comrades would not accept a peaceful end to the crisis involving their surrender. "The peaceful way out is not where we go out laying down our arms and giving up. That is impossible."
Politicians in Lima, who have supported the government's tough line with the rebels, saw the MRTA's decision to join the talks as an important step toward ending the siege.
"It's a positive move and we all have to help as much as we can to reach a happy ending," opposition legislator Antero Florez-Araoz told reporters.
Opposition congressman Harold Forsyth welcomed the creation of a commission but warned that the two sides were still far from reaching agreement. "So we have to take things cautiously," he said.
During and after the MRTA's communication, there was a flurry of activity at the residence, with both hostages and rebels appearing at the windows.
A relaxed-looking captive Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela was seen talking into a radio, while a rebel girl holding an assault rifle waved at photographers on a nearby roof.

Cerpa, who denied claims the rebels wanted ransom money for the Japanese businessmen among the hostages, said the MRTA was handling its captives with "a treatment respectful of their dignity as people."
The rebels initially took more than 500 hostages but have released most as "goodwill gestures," keeping the 74 men they consider their most valuable bargaining chips.
The remaining hostages include two Peruvian ministers, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats and the younger brother of President Alberto Fujimori.

In an internet communique, the MRTA called for supporters around the world to join its cause. "It is necessary to put pressure on Fujimori to release all our political prisoner comrades, who are hostages of the dictatorial regime," it said in a statement on its "Rebel Voice" web page.

The MRTA urged supporters to hold protests outside Peruvian embassies and consulates over the next three days and to start a letter-writing campaign to Fujimori, with copies sent to human rights organisations and the media.
